webTitle: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report

fields.headline: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report
fields.trailText: Republican senator calls bribery allegation ‘categorically false’ as ProPublica reports Trump derailed FBI inquiry
fields.bodyText: Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry. The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return. Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted. Collins has disputed the report, which her deputy chief of staff Annie Clark called “categorically false” and noted that Kao is currently in federal prison after pleading guilty to fraud charges. But it served as grist for Maine Democrats who hope they can finally convince voters to unseat Collins, who has represented the state since 1997 and survived repeated re-election challenges. “This is corruption of the highest order,” said Troy Jackson, the former state senate president and the Democratic nominee to take on Collins this year. “We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up.” Collins is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, but has a history of being a tenacious opponent. The last time Collins was on the ballot, in 2020, she beat her Democratic opponent Sara Gideon by eight percentage points, even as Joe Biden carried the state in the presidential race. Political forecasters consider her re-election campaign to be a toss-up, though recent polls have shown Jackson narrowly ahead. At a Wednesday press conference in Portland, the largest city, state Democratic party executive director Devon Murphy-Anderson accused the senator of misconduct as chair of the Senate appropriations committee, a powerful role that oversees federal spending and which Collins has used to channel significant investment to her state. “We sent Susan Collins to Washington to fight for us. Instead, it appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Murphy-Anderson said. “It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.” Addressing reporters separately, Collins’s campaign manager, Steve Abbott, denounced ProPublica’s reporting as based on “allegations from a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly”. He said that the justice department under Joe Biden had absolved the senator of the “pay-to-play” scheme that Democrats accuse her of. “In order for that claim to be true, you would have to disbelieve the Biden-led Department of Justice and the Biden-led FBI, who both investigated those contributions and the claims against Senator Collins, her campaign, and her federal staff, thoroughly, and found no basis to charge them,” Abbott said. Maine lies at the center of Democrats’ plans for retaking control of the Senate from Republicans, who won a 53-seat majority in the 2024 election. Beyond Maine, Democrats hope to win in at least three other states currently held by Republicans that voted for Trump two years ago, while also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire. Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s three most recent re-election campaigns, said the senator’s campaign in 2020 was so well-funded he found it “obviously absurd” that $150,000 would be viewed as a meaningful donation to her Super Pac. “In 2020, by the end of that race, campaigns were struggling to find places to spend money,” said Dutson, who is not involved with Collins’s re-election effort this year. He condemned ProPublica’s story as “a partisan hit piece” but said: “It’s definitely not helpful to have a story implying corruption show up in the newspaper in late September of an election year.” While Dutson argued the report is not a “silver bullet” for Collins’s foes, he warned that Trump’s low approval ratings – which have unnerved Republicans nationwide – present a significant complication for the senator’s re-election. “The headwind from Trump is very strong, as you know, and people are very upset about it,” he said. “This race is going to come down to Maine voters deciding whether that national argument is more important than the the direct relationship and the positive impact that Collins has had over the state.”

webTitle: Morning Mail: Albanese embraces Zelenskyy at UN; grocery prices climb; and ‘getting weird’ with spring fashion

fields.headline: Morning Mail: Albanese embraces Zelenskyy at UN; grocery prices climb; and ‘getting weird’ with spring fashion
fields.trailText: President says Tehran will ‘never bow’ to US in defiant speech at UN; basket of typical items increases by an average of 7%
fields.bodyText: Morning everyone. Anthony Albanese has crowned a busy day of international diplomacy by pledging another $60m in support for Ukraine at an emotional meeting in New York with the man he described fondly as “my friend” – Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy. It was no less busy elsewhere in New York as Tehran’s president ripped into Donald Trump with a defiant speech to the UN, and Argentina’s president said he would be “taking matters into his own hands” over the Falklands. None of which will help the cost of living, which a survey of typical Australian supermarket items shows is rising fast. We also report on how more young people are living with their parents, Victoria is planning more access to medical abortion, and how to dress for spring. Australia Exclusive | The Victorian government is announcing new measures to improve access to medical abortion and claims One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. ‘My friend’ | Anthony Albanese has announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN meeting in New York. Albanese will also use a speech to say that the world order is no longer fit for purpose. Grocery pain | Groceries have become more expensive at four of Australia’s major supermarket chains, with the average price of a basket of essentials increasing by 7% between March and June, analysis has found. Tax gain | Most property investors may end up paying less capital gains tax after Labor’s budget reforms, research suggests. Exclusive | The gas industry has been accused of unleashing a “scare campaign” before the Victorian election as it pressures the state government to reverse a ban on gas in new homes. Coogee rank | Coogee has once again ranked as the Sydney ocean beach most polluted with faecal matter in a survey of 245 sites across New South Wales. World Iran’s defiance | Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing America as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while also insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. The US delegation responded by walking out. The price of oil went back over $100. Donald Trump is due to welcome China’s president, Xi Jinping, and his wife for an official visit later this morning. Here’s what’s at stake when the two superpowers get down to talking. Javier Milei has condemned the UN as the Argentinian president warned that his country would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. You can follow it live here. Follow the UN meeting live. Chicken nuggets | McDonald’s is planning a global assault on KFC’s hold on the fried chicken market as more health-conscious gen Z customers shift away from beef. The burger chain is targeting an extra 1.5 percentage point share of the market. Midterm threat | Republican leaders are getting nervous as they fear Trump’s unpopularity will result in disaster at the midterms in November. Dolly fight | The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats. Full Story What Albanese has to lose from his US trip Tom McIlroy speaks to Matilda Boseley about the prime minister’s UN ambitions and what Australia has to gain if his bid for a seat on the security council succeeds. In-depth We had the intergenerational report offering a forecast of what life might be like in 40 years’ time, and now we have the Hilda report – more properly the household, income and labour dynamics survey – giving a granular update on how we live now. Patrick Commins digests the key takeaways, such as that half of Australians under 30 are living with their parents, poorly educated men aged 25-44 are being left behind, and household incomes are up but people feel less well-off. Greg Jericho digs deeper into this last point in his column. Not the news Spring has sprung and Lucianne Tonti talks to stylists and fashionistas to get some tips on sprucing up your wardrobe, including the power of tucking, a new take on knee-length skirts, and “getting weird with scarves”. Sport AFL | Immortality awaits a Fremantle side who have banished the ghosts of the club’s past, writes Brendan Foster, while Jonathan Horn profiles their “awkward outlier” of a coach, Justin Longmuir. Formula One | Lewis Hamilton said he hopes the Formula One season can still end at the two scheduled rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with the finale still in doubt because of the war in the Middle East. Football | Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. Media roundup The collapse of an “award-winning” wedding venue is concerning the Adelaide Advertiser, along with the demise of a famed country pub. A preselection challenge has ended without a single vote being cast against Moncrieff MP Angie Bell, the Bulletin reports. A newly elected mayor in FNQ wants to ban acronyms from council proceedings to improve transparency, the Cairns Post reports. The Canberra Times claims a federal agency – the National Indigenous Australians Agency – had more managers than workers until a recent round of layoffs. What’s happening today Travel woes | Qantas ground workers on a national strike for 24 hours and also a Sydney-only strike of airport security staff. Economy | ABS releases national accounts, finance and wealth, along with unemployment stats at 11.30am. Housing | National housing summit from 9am chaired by Rose Jackson. webTitle: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club

fields.headline: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
fields.trailText: Invitation announced by Marco Rubio is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and EU countries
fields.bodyText: The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.” The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies. Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club. Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”. The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries. European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit. Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended. “We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.” On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.” Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped. Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”. Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices. In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress. Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy. “President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet. For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens. On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke. A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station. Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well. In response to what has happened, the Democratic members of the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.” Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv • This article was amended on 27 September 2026 to clarify that the Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee posted the X comment on the Russia sanctions bill.

webTitle: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk

fields.headline: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
fields.trailText: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
fields.bodyText: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators. A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech. The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar. He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently. Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons. He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added. Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war. Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.” Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.” He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”. Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day. The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

webTitle: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous | Kenneth Roth

fields.headline: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous
fields.trailText: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address. For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice. He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime. In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine. Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal. He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before. Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles. Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.” He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member. He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one. Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity. Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”. It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute. Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated. He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”. Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality. He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market. He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but to hand over additional chunks of its territory as well. Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormous risks posed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.” This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”. Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

webTitle: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
fields.trailText: US-Iran meeting takes place on sidelines despite president’s threat to ‘annihilate’ Tehran regime. Plus, one man’s month-long pilates odyssey
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices. Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week. What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”. Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House. Follow UN proceedings live today here. Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump. Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July. Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day. Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16. Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” In other news … Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has set a new record, spending 23 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, unseating Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks. An US F-16 fighter jet ⁠in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, ⁠adding that one pilot had ejected safely.
